flashcards.q: What question does each of RBAC, ABAC, and ReBAC answer, and what is each one's failure mode?
flashcards.a: RBAC: 'what may this JOB FUNCTION do' -- cheapest and trivially auditable, fails by role explosion. ABAC: 'under what CONDITIONS' -- kills role explosion, fails because access is computed not stored so 'who can see X?' is O(all subjects). ReBAC: 'what RELATIONSHIP does this user have to this OBJECT' -- native cheap reverse query, fails on time-of-day / IP / MFA-level which are not relationships. They compose; they do not compete.

flashcards.q: Why is role explosion arithmetic rather than sloppiness, and what is the real fix?
flashcards.a: Role count is the PRODUCT of every dimension you encode into roles: 3 job functions x 4 regions x 3 environments x 2 data classifications = 72 roles for one conceptual job. The observable symptom is roles growing faster than headcount. The fix is not consolidation -- it is moving the exploding dimension out of the role into an attribute condition or a relationship, keeping RBAC only for the genuinely static coarse function.

flashcards.q: Give Zanzibar's production numbers from the USENIX ATC 2019 paper.
flashcards.a: More than 2 trillion relation tuples occupying ~100 TB. More than 10 million client QPS aggregate: Check peaking ~4.2M, Read 8.2M, Expand 760K, Write 25K. p95 latency under 10 ms. Availability above 99.999% over 3 years. More than 10,000 servers in several dozen clusters, median ~500 per cluster, fully replicated to more than 30 locations.

flashcards.q: What is Zanzibar's data model and its two userset rewrite rules?
flashcards.a: One tuple type: object#relation@subject, where the subject may itself be a userset like group:eng#member. Rewrites: computed_userset means a relation includes members of another relation on the SAME object (owners are editors, editors are viewers); tuple_to_userset means follow a relation to a parent object and check a relation there (a doc's viewers include its parent folder's viewers). Check is a graph traversal over that.

flashcards.q: State both flavors of the new enemy problem.
flashcards.a: 1) ACL updates applied OUT OF ORDER: Alice removes Bob from a folder, then adds a secret doc to it; a replica applying the second write first lets Bob read the doc. 2) OLD ACL applied to NEW CONTENT: Alice removes Bob from a doc, then adds sensitive content; if the content read is authorized against a pre-removal ACL snapshot, Bob reads the new content under the old permission.

flashcards.q: How does the zookie solve the new enemy problem, and why not just use strong consistency everywhere?
flashcards.a: A zookie is an opaque consistency token carrying a Spanner timestamp. The content store records it when content is written; subsequent Check calls pass it, and Zanzibar guarantees evaluation at a snapshot no earlier than that timestamp. Causal order between content and ACL updates is preserved while Zanzibar remains free to pick any LATER timestamp, which is what keeps caches hot. Strong consistency everywhere would destroy the cache and couple every check to global commit latency at 4.2M Check QPS -- so the freshness requirement was pushed into the request instead.

flashcards.q: Name the five rungs of the tenant-isolation enforcement ladder, weakest to strongest.
flashcards.a: 1) Hand-written WHERE tenant_id = ? (dies at the first background job). 2) ORM global scope (dies at raw SQL and admin tools). 3) Postgres RLS with FORCE plus SET LOCAL in an explicit transaction (the realistic target). 4) Per-tenant credentials or STS session tags (enforcement OUTSIDE the buggy process). 5) Silo, separate DB or account (dies at your ops budget, roughly 50 tenants). Every real cross-tenant leak is a path that skipped the rung the rest of the system stands on.

flashcards.q: You enabled RLS and wrote a policy, but it filters nothing. What is the #1 cause?
flashcards.a: The application connects as the role that OWNS the tables, and table owners bypass RLS by default. It is silent: the policy exists, ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is on, and every row comes back. Fix with ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY and separate the migration role (owner) from the runtime role. Other candidates: the role is superuser or has BYPASSRLS (the built-in postgres role has it and it cannot be removed).

flashcards.q: Tenant A intermittently sees tenant B's rows, only under load. Diagnose.
flashcards.a: SET app.tenant_id (session-scoped) combined with a pooler in transaction pooling mode. The setting survives on the backend connection past the transaction, so the next request borrowing that connection inherits the previous tenant's context. It only shows under load because that is when connection reuse actually happens. Fix: SET LOCAL / set_config('app.tenant_id', $1, true) inside an EXPLICIT transaction, plus a fail-closed assertion when no tenant context is set.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between USING and WITH CHECK in an RLS policy, and what breaks if you omit WITH CHECK?
flashcards.a: USING filters reads and the PRE-image of a write. WITH CHECK validates the POST-image of INSERT/UPDATE. Omit WITH CHECK and a tenant can run UPDATE ... SET tenant_id = <other tenant>, because the row was visible before the change and nothing validates it afterward. That is a write-side cross-tenant leak that read-side testing looks clean on.

flashcards.q: Name the two PostgreSQL CVEs that show RLS is not a complete boundary.
flashcards.a: CVE-2024-10976: incomplete tracking of tables with row security meant a reused query plan referenced below a subquery, WITH query, security-invoker view, or SQL-language function could view or change different rows than intended when the user ID changed. CVE-2025-8713 (disclosed 14-Aug-2025, fixed in 17.6/16.10/15.14/14.19/13.22): optimizer statistics -- histograms and most-common-values lists -- let a user read sampled data RLS intended to hide, via a crafted leaky operator. RLS constrains query RESULTS, not everything the planner will tell you about the data.

flashcards.q: List the cross-tenant leak surfaces that RLS does not cover.
flashcards.a: Cache keys without a tenant prefix; background workers running outside tenant context with an admin connection; search indexes filtered AFTER top-K instead of inside the index; object storage prefixes without a per-tenant IAM boundary; sequential IDs plus a missing object-level check (BOLA); 404-vs-403 differences acting as an existence oracle; and in multi-tenant LLM serving, a shared prefix/KV cache acting as a timing side channel across tenants.

flashcards.q: What is BOLA, why is it #1 in the API Top 10, and do UUIDs fix it?
flashcards.a: API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization: an endpoint takes an object id, fetches the object, and never checks the authenticated caller is entitled to THAT object. It is the API framing of A01 Broken Access Control (#1 in the web Top 10, 40 CWEs, 3.73% avg incidence). It is #1 because it is the default outcome of the most natural handler shape. UUIDs do NOT fix it: they raise enumeration cost and change nothing about authorization; a leaked, logged, or referrer-exposed id is still a working key.

flashcards.q: Describe NIST SP 800-207's architectural decomposition.
flashcards.a: A Policy Engine makes the decision and a Policy Administrator establishes or tears down the session credential; together they form the PDP. A Policy Enforcement Point sits in the data path in front of EVERY resource. The PE reads from identity management, device posture/CDM, PKI, activity logs, threat intel, and data access policy. Published August 2020. Every product a vendor sells you is one of those three boxes.

flashcards.q: What Zero Trust is actually deployed at scale in 2026 versus what SP 800-207 describes?
flashcards.a: Deployed: identity-aware proxies replacing VPN for internal apps (the BeyondCorp pattern), mTLS with SPIFFE/SPIRE workload identity in service meshes, device posture as a factor at authentication, and short-lived scoped credentials. Described but largely NOT deployed: continuous per-request policy re-evaluation against live risk telemetry. Most deployments evaluate richly at session establishment and then coast on a token for its lifetime.

flashcards.q: Does a completed Zero Trust rollout close your Broken Access Control risk?
flashcards.a: No, and this is the key point. Zero trust is about the NETWORK and the SESSION; object-level authorization is about the ROW. Full mTLS, device posture, identity-aware proxies, and per-session credentials do not stop GET /api/documents/8123 from returning another tenant's document when the handler fetches by id and forgets the ownership check. The PEP authorizes access to the SERVICE; A01 and BOLA live entirely behind it.

flashcards.q: Compare centralized PDP, sidecar, and in-query authorization.
flashcards.a: In-query (RLS, predicate pushdown): strongest guarantee because a code path that does not know the check exists still gets it; limited to what a SQL predicate can express. Sidecar (the OPA pattern): sub-millisecond decisions, no availability coupling, at the cost of policy distribution and N possibly-divergent copies. Centralized PDP: one auditable place to change policy, costs ~1-5 ms per decision plus a hard availability dependency. Large systems run all three at different layers; the skill is deciding which CLASS of decision goes where.

flashcards.q: Your PDP adds 4 ms p50 and you make 12 authorization calls per request. Fix it in order.
flashcards.a: 1) Batch -- every Zanzibar-derived system exposes a bulk check, so 12 calls become one. 2) Invert the query -- if you are checking 12 objects to render a list you wanted ListObjects (what can this user see), which also fixes the pagination bug where post-filtering returns short pages. 3) Cache with a bounded staleness and a real invalidation signal (SpiceDB's Watch API exists for this). Only after those three consider moving to a sidecar.

flashcards.q: When should you NOT deploy a Zanzibar-style ReBAC system?
flashcards.a: When the product has no user-to-user sharing. If permissions are 'your org's members see your org's data' and nothing else, you needed RBAC plus a tenant predicate, and you have added a distributed database, a consistency model, and an on-call rotation to solve a WHERE clause. The honest trigger for ReBAC is per-object grants with inheritance, or a genuine need for the reverse query.

flashcards.q: What is the AWS dynamically-scoped credential pattern, and what does Lambda tenant isolation mode add?
flashcards.a: Call sts:AssumeRole with a session tag carrying the tenant id, then condition the IAM policy on aws:PrincipalTag/tenant (for example against dynamodb:LeadingKeys), so the credential the code holds physically cannot reach another tenant's data even when the query is wrong -- rung 4 implemented in IAM, outside the buggy process. Lambda tenant isolation mode (announced Nov-2025, all regions except ap-southeast New Zealand, GovCloud, and China): pass a tenant identifier at invoke and Lambda guarantees an execution environment is never reused across tenants. Cost: cold starts multiply by active tenant count, so it fits high-value low-cardinality tenants and not a long tail.

flashcards.q: How does authorization change when an AI agent acts on a user's behalf?
flashcards.a: The request no longer has one principal. The decision becomes an intersection: the agent may do X only if the USER may do X, AND the agent's own delegated grant permits X, AND context conditions hold. The working pieces: per-agent identity rather than sharing the user's credential, a delegated short-TTL credential scoped to a subset of the user's permissions (OAuth token exchange, RFC 8693, is the closest standard), tool allowlisting at the gateway rather than in the prompt, and human confirmation on irreversible actions. Re-delegation to sub-agents has no standard answer: mint sub-agent credentials from the original user grant with strictly smaller scope, never pass the parent's credential down.
